draft_text:
There is a photograph by Peter Hujar — *David Wojnarowicz (Hand Touching Eye)*, 1981 — in which a hand reaches toward a face, fingers half-obscuring the gaze. It is a picture about seeing and being seen, about the vulnerability of the act itself. That Gropius Bau chose this image to lead the publicity for *Persistence of Vision* tells you something about curatorial intent. This is not a retrospective that treats Hujar as a sainted martyr of the downtown scene. It is an exhibition about what happens when you look, and what the medium of photography does to the looking.

Opening on 18 March, *Peter Hujar / Liz Deschenes: Persistence of Vision* brings together around 120 of Hujar's photographs — [~many shown for the first time in Berlin|this claim comes directly from Gropius Bau's own materials; I haven't found independent confirmation of which specific works are new to the city~] — alongside sculptural and photographic works by Liz Deschenes. The pairing is not obvious. Hujar, who died of AIDS-related illness in 1987 at fifty-three, made fiercely intimate black-and-white portraits of the people and places that constituted New York's queer and artistic underground between Stonewall and the plague years. Deschenes, born in 1966, makes work that barely resembles photography in any conventional sense: photograms exposed to moonlight, glass sculptures that shift with the viewer's position, surfaces that continue to oxidise long after they leave the darkroom. One artist gave us Candy Darling on her deathbed. The other gives us silver paper slowly changing in ambient light. The exhibition argues these practices share a root.

Hujar's biography reads like a compressed history of mid-century American photography itself. Raised by Ukrainian immigrant grandparents in rural New Jersey, he picked up his mother's camera as a child and never really put it down. A move to New York at twelve, a Fulbright to Italy in 1962, a visit to the Palermo Catacombs with the artist Paul Thek that seeded a lifelong obsession with mortality. A masterclass with Richard Avedon in 1967 that pushed him to abandon commercial work entirely. By the 1970s he was living and working in the East Village, making portraits of Susan Sontag, William S. Burroughs, Fran Lebowitz, Wojnarowicz — a circle that reads now as a who's-who of American countercultural life but at the time was simply the neighbourhood. Hujar's great skill was a refusal to mythologise. His subjects look back at the camera with a directness that feels almost confrontational, stripped of the soft-focus romanticism that plagued so much queer portraiture of the era. He once said he made "uncomplicated, direct photographs of complicated and difficult subjects." That clarity is the thread the curators pull on.

Deschenes' work requires a different kind of attention. Trained at Rhode Island School of Design, she has spent decades interrogating what a photograph actually is at the level of material: light hitting a chemically sensitive surface, time passing, oxidation accumulating. Her *Elevations* and *Green Screen* series treat colour as subject rather than attribute, producing monochrome works that sit ambiguously between image and object. More recent photograms are made by exposing paper to natural and artificial light outdoors at night — no camera, no lens, no subject in the traditional sense. The resulting surfaces are silvery, tonal, shifting. Some of her glass works have no photographic component at all, yet they engage the same questions about perception, reflection, and the instability of what we think we see.

The curatorial logic, then, is not biographical but phenomenological. Both artists are interested in what photography does before it becomes a picture of something. For Hujar, the decisive act was the encounter — the charged space between his lens and a living face, a dying animal, a crumbling wall. For Deschenes, it is the medium's own physics: photons, silver halide, entropy. [~The curators — Eva Respini of Vancouver Art Gallery and Monique Machicao y Priemer Ferrufino of Gropius Bau — have structured the exhibition so that Deschenes' works are interspersed among Hujar's photographs as "interludes"|sourced consistently across all Gropius Bau materials and the Peter Hujar Archive listing~], punctuation marks that ask the viewer to slow down, to become conscious of the act of looking between one image and the next. The architecture of Gropius Bau — that Italian Neo-Renaissance shell rebuilt from wartime ruin, where reconstructed mosaics sit alongside deliberately exposed gaps in the masonry — becomes a third presence. A building that carries its own damage visibly is a pointed context for work concerned with light, loss, and what persists.

It matters that this is happening in Berlin, and it matters that it is happening now. Hujar has had a strange posthumous trajectory. Largely underappreciated during his lifetime — he published one book, *Portraits in Life and Death*, in 1976, with an essay by Susan Sontag, and it did not sell — he was gradually canonised in the decades after his death, as the cultural significance of the downtown New York scene he documented became impossible to ignore. [~Major retrospectives have appeared at the Morgan Library (2017) and Fundación MAPFRE in Madrid, among others, but Berlin has until now lacked a comprehensive showing|based on exhibition history available through the Peter Hujar Archive and institutional listings; coverage is solid~]. That the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn is simultaneously presenting *Peter Hujar: Eyes Open in the Dark* from February to August 2026 suggests a coordinated German institutional commitment to the work — a dual-city moment that positions Hujar within European photographic discourse rather than leaving him as a chapter in New York art history.

Deschenes' inclusion complicates any temptation to treat the show as pure memorial. Her work resists nostalgia structurally. You cannot be sentimental about a photogram exposed to moonlight; it has no face, no story, no death. What it has is a relationship to time that is ongoing — oxidation means the work is literally still changing on the wall. Placed beside Hujar's portraits of people many of whom died young, this temporal instability becomes its own kind of elegy: not for a person, but for the idea that any image is ever finished.

What the visitor will encounter, concretely, is a show that moves between the figural and the abstract, between recognition and estrangement. Hujar's images — animals, ruins, nudes, the famous faces and the unknown ones — are presented across all phases of his career, from early 1950s experiments to the final studio works. Deschenes' glass pieces introduce literal reflection: the viewer sees themselves, the room, other visitors, folded into the surface of the artwork. A DJ set accompanies the free opening evening on 18 March, a gesture toward sociability that echoes Hujar's own immersion in a scene where art, music, and nightlife were not separate categories.

[~The phrase "persistence of vision" itself is borrowed from optics — the phenomenon by which the retina retains an image briefly after the source is gone|this is a standard definition; the curators clearly chose it for its double meaning~]. It is what makes cinema possible: the brain stitches still frames into continuous motion because each image lingers a fraction of a second beyond its exposure. As a title for an exhibition pairing a dead photographer with a living one, it suggests that what we see does not end when we look away. The afterimage remains. In a building that once burned and was rebuilt, in a city defined by the gap between what was and what is, that idea carries weight no press release needs to spell out.
critique_assessment: Publishable with minor revisions — the essay has genuine insight and strong structure, but needs factual corrections, a few voice tightenings, and one instance of decorative name-dropping trimmed.

critique_issues.fix: The source says 'A Fulbright scholarship took him to Italy in 1962, where he studied film and travelled extensively.' The essay calls it simply 'a Fulbright to Italy' which is fine, but then says 'a visit to the Palermo Catacombs with the artist Paul Thek that seeded a lifelong obsession with mortality.' The source material mentions the Italy trip deepening 'his lifelong engagement with mortality' but says nothing about the Palermo Catacombs or Paul Thek being on that trip. The Thek-Catacombs connection is well-documented in Hujar scholarship elsewhere, but the Palermo detail and its timing are suspiciously specific for what the sources provide. Flag and soften — attribute the Catacombs visit to general Hujar lore rather than presenting it as established fact, or add a confidence marker.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3: 'A masterclass with Richard Avedon in 1967'
critique_issues.fix: Not in the source material provided. This is widely cited in Hujar biographies but should carry a confidence marker since we can't verify it from the materials at hand.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3: 'He once said he made "uncomplicated, direct photographs of complicated and difficult subjects."'
critique_issues.fix: This is a well-known Hujar quote but no source is provided here. It should either get a confidence marker or be attributed more carefully (e.g., 'as he reportedly described his practice').

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6: 'Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn is simultaneously presenting Peter Hujar: Eyes Open in the Dark from February to August 2026'
critique_issues.fix: Not verifiable from the source material provided. This is plausible — there was indeed a Bundeskunsthalle Hujar show announced — but the specific dates and title should carry a confidence marker.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3: the long biographical paragraph listing Sontag, Burroughs, Lebowitz, Wojnarowicz
critique_issues.fix: The sentence 'a circle that reads now as a who's-who of American countercultural life but at the time was simply the neighbourhood' is a nice observation, but the list itself is four names long and starts to feel like a Wikipedia roll call. Cut one or two — Lebowitz and Burroughs are not essential to the argument. The essay already mentions Wojnarowicz and Candy Darling; Sontag appears later re: the book. Trim.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 2: 'One artist gave us Candy Darling on her deathbed. The other gives us silver paper slowly changing in ambient light.'
critique_issues.fix: This is strong rhetoric but 'gave us' is slightly cloying — as if the artists exist to serve us images. Consider 'One made' / 'The other makes' for directness.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 8: 'What the visitor will encounter, concretely...'
critique_issues.fix: This paragraph sags. After the strong phenomenological argument in paragraphs 5-7, dropping into 'what you'll see' mode feels like a press release appendix. The concrete details (all phases of career, glass pieces introducing reflection, DJ set) should be folded earlier into the essay where they serve the argument. The DJ set detail is interesting but it's buried and tossed off.

The Deschenes paragraph is solid but slightly more descriptive than analytical. The Hujar sections have a clear point of view ('His great skill was a refusal to mythologise'). Deschenes gets described but not evaluated with the same confidence. Push harder — what is the critical claim about her work?

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6: 'a dual-city moment that positions Hujar within European photographic discourse rather than leaving him as a chapter in New York art history'
Final paragraph: 'that idea carries weight no press release needs to spell out'
critique_issues.fix: Slightly smug closer — as if the essay is congratulating itself for not being a press release while still ending on a somewhat press-release-worthy note about Berlin and memory. The final sentence should be sharper or cut.

research_context.venue_context: During the Second World War the building was badly damaged during air raids on Berlin. The roof and collection holdings in the basement were reduced to ashes; the northern facade and upper floors were almost completely destroyed. The ruins were left to decay until the 1960s, when the planned demolition was averted by the great nephew of its creator, architect and Bauhaus founder Walter Gropius.
